senses.def: a system for sending messages between computers, or a message sent this way
examples: I got an email from my landlord about the rent increase.
Please send your application by email before Friday.

senses.def: to send a message or a file to someone by email
examples: Can you email me the slides after the meeting?
She emailed the whole team to cancel the call.

note: Also spelled "e-mail". In speech, Americans often just say "I'll send it to you" or "I'll shoot you an email" (informal).

senses.tr: (yeni ve zor bir işe) girişmek, başlamak
senses.def: to start something new, important, or difficult (used with on or upon)
examples: After college, she embarked on a career in journalism.
The city is embarking on an ambitious plan to rebuild its subway.

senses.def: to get onto a ship or plane at the start of a journey
examples: Passengers began to embark at the port just after dawn.

note: The "start" sense is far more common and always takes "on/upon": embark on a new venture.

senses.def: feeling uncomfortable or ashamed, especially because of what other people think of you
examples: I was so embarrassed when I called my teacher "Mom" in class.
He felt embarrassed about forgetting her name.

note: Spelled with double r and double s. Embarrassed = how you feel; embarrassing = the situation that causes it. Not the same as "ashamed" (guilt).

senses.def: making you feel uncomfortable, silly, or ashamed in front of others
examples: It was embarrassing to trip on stage in front of the whole school.
The leaked emails were deeply embarrassing for the company.

note: -ing describes the cause (an embarrassing question); -ed describes the person's feeling (I was embarrassed).

senses.def: the uncomfortable feeling you have when you are ashamed or feel silly in front of others
examples: His face turned red with embarrassment.
To my embarrassment, my phone rang during the funeral.

senses.def: a person or thing that makes others feel ashamed
examples: The failed launch was a major embarrassment for the government.

senses.def: the official building or group of diplomats that represents a country in a foreign capital
examples: She went to the embassy to apply for a student visa.
Protesters gathered outside the US embassy in the capital.

note: An embassy is in the capital; a consulate (konsolosluk) is a smaller office in other cities.

senses.def: to fix something firmly inside a surrounding material or object
examples: A piece of glass was embedded in his foot.
The fossils are embedded in layers of rock.

senses.tr: (fikir, kültür vb.) kök salmak, yerleşmek; (web) yerleştirmek
senses.def: to make an idea or habit a deep part of something; to put a video, link, etc. into a web page
examples: Racism is deeply embedded in some institutions.
You can embed the video directly on your blog.

note: Very often used in the passive: "be embedded in". The doubled d appears in embedded, embedding.

senses.tr: somutlaştırmak, temsil etmek, -in vücut bulmuş hali olmak
senses.def: to express or represent an idea or quality clearly and completely
examples: For many fans, the team captain embodies the spirit of the club.
The new constitution embodies the values of freedom and equality.

note: "The embodiment of" is common: she is the embodiment of kindness (iyiliğin vücut bulmuş hali).

senses.def: to put your arms around someone to show love or friendship
examples: The two brothers embraced at the airport after ten years apart.

senses.def: to accept a new idea, belief, or change willingly and with enthusiasm
examples: Many older workers have embraced remote work.
The town has embraced tourism as a source of income.

senses.def: the act of holding someone close in your arms
examples: She greeted her grandson with a warm embrace.

note: In everyday speech "hug" is the usual word for the physical act; "embrace" sounds more formal or literary.

senses.def: to come out from a hidden or dark place and become visible
examples: A deer emerged from the trees and crossed the road.
The sun emerged from behind the clouds.

senses.def: to become known, especially after being hidden or unclear
examples: It later emerged that the mayor had known about the problem.
New details have emerged about the crash.

senses.def: to start to exist or become important; to come out of a difficult situation
examples: Several new tech hubs have emerged in the Midwest.
The company emerged from bankruptcy stronger than before.

note: "Emerging markets" (gelişmekte olan piyasalar) is a very frequent economics phrase.

senses.def: the process of appearing, starting to exist, or becoming known or important
examples: The emergence of smartphones changed how people read the news.
Scientists are tracking the emergence of a new virus strain.

note: Do not confuse with "emergency" (acil durum).

senses.def: a sudden, serious, dangerous situation that needs action immediately
examples: In an emergency, call 911.
The plane made an emergency landing after one engine failed.

note: American: "emergency room (ER)" = acil servis. The British say "A&E". In the US you dial 911.

senses.def: the release of gas, heat, light, etc. into the air, or an amount that is released
examples: The new law aims to cut carbon emissions by half by 2035.
Cars must pass an emissions test every two years.

note: Usually plural (emissions) when talking about pollution.

senses.def: a strong feeling such as love, fear, or anger, or feelings in general as opposed to reason
examples: She tried hard to hide her emotions during the interview.
His voice was full of emotion as he thanked his parents.

senses.def: connected with people's feelings
examples: Children need emotional support as well as food and shelter.
Losing a job can take a huge emotional toll.

senses.def: showing strong feelings, often by crying; causing strong feelings
examples: He got very emotional during his farewell speech.
Immigration remains an emotional issue for many voters.

senses.def: in a way that is connected with feelings, or in a way that shows strong feeling
examples: Caring for a sick parent can be emotionally exhausting.
She spoke emotionally about her years in the refugee camp.

senses.def: special importance or attention given to something
examples: The school puts a strong emphasis on reading and writing.
There is now more emphasis on prevention than treatment.

senses.def: extra force given to a word or syllable when speaking
examples: She said "never" with heavy emphasis.

note: Plural: emphases. Use "emphasis on" (not "to"): The emphasis is on quality.

senses.def: to show or say that something is especially important
examples: The doctor emphasized the need for regular exercise.
I want to emphasize that nobody will lose their job.

note: No preposition: emphasize something (NOT emphasize on something). British spelling: emphasise.

senses.def: a group of countries controlled by one ruler or government
examples: The Ottoman Empire lasted for more than six centuries.
At its height, the Roman Empire stretched from Britain to Egypt.

senses.def: a large group of businesses controlled by one person or company
examples: He built a media empire from a single local newspaper.

senses.def: based on observation, experiments, or experience rather than theory
examples: There is little empirical evidence that the diet works.
The study offers an empirical analysis of wage data from 40 countries.

note: Academic word. Opposite: theoretical.

senses.def: to pay someone to work for you
examples: The factory employs about 300 people from the town.
She is employed as a nurse at the local hospital.

senses.def: to use a particular method, skill, or tool (formal)
examples: The researchers employed a range of techniques to collect data.

note: In everyday speech, "hire" is more common for taking on a new worker.

senses.def: a person who is paid to work for a company or another person
examples: The company gave every employee a bonus at the end of the year.
Part-time employees are not eligible for health insurance.

note: Employee = the person who works; employer = the person or company that pays. Stress is on the last syllable for many speakers.

senses.def: a person or organization that pays people to work for them
examples: The hospital is the largest employer in the county.
Ask your employer whether they offer a retirement plan.

senses.def: paid work, or the state of having a paid job
examples: Many graduates struggle to find employment in their field.
Employment in manufacturing has fallen sharply since the 1980s.

senses.def: the use of something for a particular purpose (formal)
examples: The employment of new teaching methods improved test scores.

senses.def: to give someone the power, confidence, or legal right to do something
examples: The program aims to empower women to start their own businesses.
The new law empowers police to stop and search vehicles.

senses.def: with nobody or nothing inside
examples: The streets were empty at three in the morning.
Don't put the empty milk carton back in the fridge.

senses.def: having no real meaning, value, or purpose
examples: Voters are tired of empty promises.
After the divorce, his life felt empty.

senses.def: to remove everything from a container or place, or to become empty
examples: Could you empty the dishwasher before you go?
The stadium emptied quickly after the final whistle.

note: "On an empty stomach" = aç karnına. "Vacant" is used for seats, rooms, and jobs.

senses.def: to make it possible for someone to do something or for something to happen
examples: The scholarship enabled her to study abroad.
New software enables doctors to share records instantly.

senses.def: to turn on a feature or function on a computer or device
examples: You need to enable cookies to use this website.

note: Pattern: enable + object + to-infinitive (enable us to save time), NOT enable to do.

senses.def: to make a proposal into law
examples: Congress enacted the law with support from both parties.
Several states have enacted stricter gun laws.

senses.def: to perform a story or scene, for example in a play (formal)
examples: The students enacted a scene from the trial.

note: Formal, used in law and politics.

senses.def: to include a wide range of things or ideas
examples: The course encompasses both ancient and modern history.
Her job encompasses everything from hiring to payroll.

senses.def: to surround an area completely
examples: The national park encompasses three lakes and a large forest.

senses.def: to experience something, especially a problem or something difficult
examples: We encountered heavy traffic on the way to the airport.
Please call us if you encounter any problems with the app.

senses.def: to meet someone or see something, especially unexpectedly
examples: It was the strangest animal she had ever encountered.

senses.def: a meeting, often a sudden or unexpected one, or a brief experience of something
examples: He described his close encounter with a bear in Alaska.
A chance encounter on a train changed her life.

note: Formal for "run into" or "come across". Pattern: encounter something (no preposition).

senses.def: to give someone support, confidence, or hope so they will do something
examples: My parents always encouraged me to follow my dreams.
Teachers should encourage students to ask questions.

senses.def: to make something more likely to happen or develop
examples: Low interest rates encourage people to borrow more.
The city wants to encourage the use of public transit.

senses.def: words or actions that give someone confidence or hope to do something
examples: With her coach's encouragement, she entered the marathon.
Shy children need a lot of encouragement to speak in class.

senses.def: giving you hope or confidence that something will succeed
examples: The early results of the trial are very encouraging.
It's encouraging to see so many young people voting.

senses.def: the final part of a period of time, event, activity, or story
examples: We're moving to Denver at the end of the month.
I didn't understand the end of the movie.

senses.def: the furthest point or part of something long
examples: Our house is at the end of the street.

senses.tr: bitmek, sona ermek; bitirmek, sona erdirmek
senses.def: to finish, or to make something finish
examples: The meeting ended with a vote.
Both sides want to end the war.

note: "In the end" = eventually (sonunda); "at the end (of)" = at the final point of. "End up" = to finally be in a situation.

senses.def: a serious attempt to do something new or difficult (formal)
examples: Space exploration is one of humanity's greatest endeavors.
We wish you success in all your future endeavors.

senses.def: to try very hard to do something (formal)
examples: We will endeavor to answer every email within 24 hours.

note: British spelling: endeavour. Formal; in speech, use "try" or "effort".

senses.def: the last part of a story, movie, or event
examples: I love books with a happy ending.
The show's ending left many viewers disappointed.

senses.def: the last part of a word, such as -ed or -ing
examples: Past tense verbs usually take the ending -ed.

senses.def: very large in size or amount, or seeming never to stop
examples: I'm tired of endless meetings that achieve nothing.
The desert seemed to stretch into an endless horizon.

senses.def: to say publicly that you support a person, idea, or plan
examples: The newspaper endorsed her for governor.
The committee endorsed the proposal unanimously.

senses.def: to say in an advertisement that you use and like a product
examples: Famous athletes are paid millions to endorse sneakers.

senses.def: a public statement of support for a person, idea, or plan
examples: The senator won the endorsement of the largest teachers' union.
The plan received a strong endorsement from economists.

senses.def: a deal in which a well-known person promotes a product for money
examples: The tennis star earns more from endorsements than from prize money.

senses.def: to experience and deal with something painful or unpleasant for a long time
examples: The refugees endured weeks of hunger and cold.
She had to endure years of criticism before her work was accepted.

senses.def: to continue to exist for a long time (formal)
examples: Their friendship endured for over sixty years.

senses.def: a person who hates or opposes someone and tries to harm them
examples: He made a lot of enemies during his time as mayor.
The two families have been bitter enemies for generations.

senses.def: a country or army that you are fighting in a war
examples: The soldiers were captured behind enemy lines.

note: Opposite: friend, ally. "Your own worst enemy" = someone who causes their own problems.

senses.def: the physical and mental strength and enthusiasm you need to be active
examples: I don't have the energy to cook tonight.
Kids have so much energy in the morning.

senses.def: power from electricity, fuel, the sun, etc. used to run machines and heat buildings
examples: The country gets most of its energy from wind and solar power.
Energy prices rose sharply last winter.

senses.def: to make sure that people obey a law or rule
examples: Police are now strictly enforcing the speed limit near schools.
The rule is rarely enforced.

senses.def: to make something happen or force a situation to exist
examples: You can't enforce discipline by shouting at people.

senses.def: the act of making people obey a law or rule
examples: Stricter enforcement of traffic laws has reduced accidents.
Local law enforcement officers arrived within minutes.

note: In American English "law enforcement" often means the police and similar agencies (kolluk kuvvetleri).

senses.def: to attract and keep someone's interest or attention
examples: A good teacher knows how to engage a room full of teenagers.
The museum uses games to engage young visitors.

senses.def: to take part in an activity or become involved with someone (engage in / with)
examples: Students who engage in sports tend to do better at school.
The company needs to engage more with its customers.

senses.def: to employ someone for a particular job (formal)
examples: They engaged a lawyer to handle the sale of the house.

senses.def: having formally agreed to marry someone
examples: They got engaged last summer and plan to marry in June.
She's engaged to a doctor from Chicago.

senses.def: busy with or actively involved in something
examples: Students learn more when they are actively engaged in the lesson.

note: "Engaged to" (not "with") someone. In British English a phone line can be "engaged"; Americans say "busy".

senses.def: an agreement to marry someone, or the period before the wedding
examples: They announced their engagement at a family dinner.
He gave her an antique engagement ring.

senses.def: the act of being involved with or interested in something
examples: The new app increased user engagement by 30 percent.

senses.def: an arrangement to do something or meet someone, especially officially
examples: The minister had to cancel several speaking engagements.

senses.def: interesting or pleasant in a way that attracts and holds your attention
examples: She's an engaging speaker who keeps the audience laughing.
The book is an engaging account of life on a farm.

senses.def: the part of a vehicle or machine that produces power to make it move
examples: The car's engine wouldn't start on the cold morning.
One of the plane's engines caught fire shortly after takeoff.

senses.def: a vehicle that pulls a train
examples: The old steam engine pulled six passenger cars.

note: "Search engine" = arama motoru. "Motor" is used for smaller electric machines; cars have engines.

senses.def: a person whose job is designing and building machines, structures, systems, or software
examples: She works as a software engineer at a startup in Austin.
Civil engineers inspected the bridge after the earthquake.

senses.def: a person who drives a train or repairs and controls engines
examples: The train's engineer hit the brakes when he saw the car on the tracks.

senses.def: to design and build something, or to arrange something cleverly or secretly
examples: The crops have been genetically engineered to resist pests.
Critics say the crisis was engineered for political gain.

note: In American English the driver of a train is also called an "engineer".
